brief.text: A friend of Ajay Shah’s says the heart is a solved prob­lem. Biologically, yes, Amit Varma replied, but metaphor­i­cally “no one can solve the heart.” {086-J17}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma’s stent, and the rebels who made it possible
lead.head: Rebels with a catheter

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 86

body: Amit Varma came to the stu­dio in a full-sleeve shirt, and after a joke about show­ing too much skin, ex­plained why. Half his arm had been shaved for an an­gio­plasty.

A few days ear­lier he had been told that he had had a minor heart at­tack, and had not no­ticed. A CT scan found an 80 to 90 per cent block in his right coro­nary artery. By the time of the pro­ce­dure it was 100 per cent. {086-S01}

He had blamed dust, COVID and food poi­son­ing for weeks of acid­ity, vom­it­ing and a tight chest. “The way I imag­ine a heart at­tack is that there’s a dra­matic mo­ment, back­ground music in­creases,” he said. “There was noth­ing dra­matic.”
For Ajay Shah, it was per­sonal. His fa­ther had a small heart at­tack in 1982 that was recog­nised as one only a month later. He died of a sec­ond in 1984, aged 58. {086-S03}
## Rethink, don’t pol­ish

In hos­pi­tal, Varma had been read­ing about DeepSeek, and a line from a thread by Morgan Brown gave him the episode: in­cum­bents op­ti­mise ex­ist­ing pro­cesses, while dis­rup­tors re­think the fun­da­men­tal ap­proach.
“The only thing that leads to human progress is re­think­ing the fun­da­men­tals,” he said. “There’s ab­so­lutely noth­ing else.” {086-C01}
The peo­ple who do it, he said, are ma­ligned and treated like heretics, above all by those Paul Graham calls the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional minded.
Medicine sup­plied the first of them. In Berlin in 1929, Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doc­tor, guided a catheter into his own heart.

In Australia, Barry Marshall drank water laced with the bac­terium be­hind stom­ach ul­cers to prove they were an in­fec­tion. Charles Dotter built catheters in his kitchen, and in 1977 Andreas Gruentzig per­formed the first coro­nary an­gio­plasty.
## Cricket, couches and Bombay
Cricket sup­plied Sri Lanka, un­der­dogs who won the 1996 World Cup by send­ing two lower-order bats­men to open and at­tack from the first ball.
Strategy lags a change of for­mat by years or even decades, Varma ar­gued, and even after a heretic is proved right, adop­tion is slow.

Business sup­plied Netflix, which beat Blockbuster by post­ing DVDs with­out late fees, then moved into stream­ing in 2007, be­fore the tech­nol­ogy seemed ready. Its rea­son­ing, as Varma put it: “If we don’t do it, some­body else will, and our busi­ness will get over.” {086-S10}
Varma’s own story was of being too early. In 2000 he pitched New York in­vestors what was “ba­si­cally MySpace” and “ba­si­cally iTunes”, from Bombay. Then the Nasdaq crashed. {086-S12}
Thinking out­side the box, he con­cluded, is nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient. You also need luck, and the per­sis­tence to give it more chances.
## Breeding heretics

Ajay Shah asked where such dis­rup­tors come from, and an­swered with four pil­lars: a cul­ture of ir­rev­er­ence, gate­keep­ers who re­ward nov­elty, a so­ci­ety that hon­ours fail­ure, and tol­er­ance for peo­ple who are not nice. “More sti­fling so­ci­eties just make stul­ti­fied peo­ple,” he said.
Varma noted that Shah had thereby im­plied he was not a nice guy, a weirdo and one of the nut­cases. He ac­cepted all of it.
The hosts ended on ma­chines. Varma quoted a reply to a ques­tion by the pod­caster Dwarkesh Patel: “To an LLM, a novel dis­cov­ery is in­dis­tin­guish­able from an error.”
The human edge, Varma said, is to dive into what is new with­out as­sum­ing that what has not been said be­fore must be crap.

second.label: Medicine
second.head: He drank the evidence
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the Australian doctor who gave himself ulcers to prove their cause
body: Stomach ul­cers were once treated as a de­gen­er­a­tive dis­ease of old age, like choles­terol, Ajay Shah said. There was no cure: only bland food and avoid­ing stress, and peo­ple died hor­ri­ble deaths.

In Australia, Barry Marshall ar­gued that ul­cers were a sim­ple in­fec­tious dis­ease, and no­body ac­cepted it. To meet Koch’s pos­tu­lates, he ex­per­i­mented on him­self: he scoped his own healthy stom­ach, drank water con­tain­ing Helicobacter py­lori and scoped again to show full-blown ul­cers.

A sim­ple course of an­tibi­otics cleared them, which a third look con­firmed. {086-S05} Marshall won the 2005 Nobel Prize for Medicine. {#nobel2005} “You need the ge­nius mad men with con­vic­tion,” Amit Varma said.

quote.text: He de­lib­er­ately took the bac­te­ria into his own body and went through the course of an­tibi­otics and it got cleared up.

third.head: Fangs, but no fanfare

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the snake bite you barely feel

body: Heart at­tacks are not the only killers that come with­out drama. Ajay Shah of­fered the bite of a ven­omous snake as an anal­ogy.
As a city child, he said, he imag­ined a cobra bite as a cat­a­clysm: the fangs grip­ping your calf, and a few mo­ments later you keel over dead.

In fact, he said, such snakes bite at high speed, pump venom in like a hy­po­der­mic sy­ringe and get far away. {086-S02} The vic­tim feels very lit­tle and may see only two punc­ture marks, while the drama plays out over min­utes and hours. Victims of com­mon krait bites are bit­ten in their sleep and found dead in the morn­ing.
Amit Varma pic­tured the Shah and Thomas house­hold at night, with Shah wak­ing to ask, “Susan, did you bite me just now?” {086-J06}

box.title: The thread behind the episode
box.text: Paul Graham’s essay *The Four Quadrants of Conformism* named the enemy: the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional minded. The the­sis came from a thread on DeepSeek by Morgan Brown, which Amit Varma read in hos­pi­tal: “Incumbents op­ti­mize ex­ist­ing pro­cesses while dis­rup­tors re­think the fun­da­men­tal ap­proach.” {086-R02}

sections.label: Medicine, part one
sections.head: Pac-Man in the arteries
sections.caption: the procedure he watched on three screens
body: Amit Varma ex­plained his pro­ce­dure be­fore its his­tory. Doctors made an in­ser­tion in the ra­dial artery, put in a sheath and ran a guide wire all the way to the heart. Along it went a catheter, a thin tube that can carry dye or a bal­loon.
In his case the bal­loon car­ried a drug-eluting stent. The bal­loon ex­panded, the stent ex­panded with it, and the bal­loon came out, leav­ing the stent in place.

He lay be­side three screens, like a day trader’s, while a doc­tor worked what was prac­ti­cally a video-game con­troller. “Like in a game of Pac-Man,” he said, they ma­noeu­vred through his ar­ter­ies zap­ping clots, then dealt with a block that had reached 100 per cent. {086-J16}
It was all over in an hour. “So mirac­u­lous,” he said.
## Nowhere near the heart

In 1929, Varma said, the con­ven­tional wis­dom was to take a catheter nowhere near the heart. In a leg, where ar­ter­ies are wider, the worst out­come was los­ing the leg. The heart was too sen­si­tive.

Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doc­tor in Berlin, went ahead on him­self. His boss at the next hos­pi­tal, Ferdinand Sauerbruch, was Varma’s ex­am­ple of the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional minded. {086-J15} The phrase is Paul Graham’s, for peo­ple to whom a chal­lenge to con­ven­tion feels like a per­sonal af­front. {086-C02}
~ Had Forssmann died on the table, Varma said, mod­ern sci­ence would have got there any­way. “But we would not know the name of that dude.” {#noname}

quote.text: With such ex­per­i­ments you might ha­bil­i­tate in a cir­cus, but these have no place in a de­cent German hos­pi­tal.
quote.who: Ferdinand Sauerbruch, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Medicine, part two
sections.head: The plumber and the diplomat
sections.caption: two pioneers of angioplasty
body: Charles Dotter, who pi­o­neered an­gio­plasty in other parts of the body from the 1960s, was openly re­bel­lious, Amit Varma said. He went to first prin­ci­ples: the heart is, after all, a phys­i­cal ob­ject.
His favourite “con­cep­tual trade­mark” was a sketch of a crossed pipe and wrench. If a plumber can do it to pipes, Dotter said, “we can do it to blood ves­sels.” {#plumber}
Varma used a dis­tinc­tion Ajay Shah once drew be­tween tech­ni­cians, trained in pro­ce­dures, and thinkers, who ques­tion them. Dotter was both. {086-C03}
## Playing the sys­tem
Andreas Gruentzig, much younger, thought the same way with the op­po­site tem­per­a­ment. He knew you had to play the sys­tem and be po­lite to ev­ery­one. {086-S07}

Why open the heart for a by­pass, he asked, when a catheter could carry a bal­loon to the block­age? Textbooks and top sur­geons warned of ven­tric­u­lar fib­ril­la­tion and death within min­utes. In 1977 he went ahead, on around six pa­tients, and his talk won a stand­ing ova­tion. {#sixpatients}
Stents met the same re­sis­tance, be­cause once one is in the heart it can­not be re­moved. They ar­rived in the 1980s and were rou­tine by the mid-1990s.
~ Only partly in­sured, Varma saw his bill and imag­ined a per­pet­ual heart at­tack ma­chine. Shah di­ag­nosed Zeno-phobia: “the ir­ra­tional fear of con­ver­gent se­quences”. {086-J07}

quote.text: Gruentzig is a guy who knows that you gotta play the sys­tem, that you gotta write the pa­pers in the right order

sections.label: Sport
sections.head: Bang bang bang from ball one
sections.caption: Sri Lanka’s 1996 heresy
body: Sri Lanka came to the 1996 World Cup as un­der­dogs, much like India in 1983. The ex­am­ple came to Amit Varma from Pranay Kotasthane.

The tem­plate of the day had open­ers build, the mid­dle order con­sol­i­date and ev­ery­one slog in the last ten overs. With field re­stric­tions mak­ing early bound­aries more prof­itable, Sri Lanka sent two lower-order bats­men, Romesh Kaluwitharana and Sanath Jayasuriya, out to open and at­tack. They took the Cup. {086-S08}

Strategy is slow to catch up with a new for­mat, Varma ar­gued. When one-day cricket ar­rived, Sunil Gavaskar made 36 not out in a 60-over match at the 1975 World Cup, play­ing to Test rhythms. {#gavaskar}
## The price of a dot ball

In T20 the same eleven bats­men get only twenty overs. That raises the cost of a dot ball and low­ers the cost of a wicket, so the ex­pected value of ag­gres­sion rises. {086-C05} Send the hit­ters out first, Varma said, and keep the an­chor for emer­gen­cies.
England later ap­plied the logic to one-day cricket, and 300-plus scores, once com­mon mainly on the subcontinent’s flat pitches, be­came com­mon ev­ery­where. {#england300}
~ Around 2016 Varma told a poker friend who bet on cricket to back the team bat­ting sec­ond in the IPL. After four­teen games, the chas­ing side had won thir­teen. {#thirteen}

quote.text: We will ask them to open the in­nings and we will ask them to go bang bang bang from the start.

sections.label: Movies
sections.head: First Blockbuster, then itself
sections.caption: how Netflix disrupted itself
body: Amit Varma often crit­i­cises Netflix for what it does in India. Its ori­gin story, he said, is a bril­liant ex­am­ple of a com­pany that dis­rupted oth­ers and was not dis­rupted it­self.
In the late 1990s Blockbuster ruled American home video: a store with a lim­ited col­lec­tion, and late fees, “pun­ish­ing the Bengali pro­cras­ti­na­tor”. {086-J11}

From 1997 Netflix posted DVDs with no late fees, soon on a monthly sub­scrip­tion, with a cat­a­logue brows­able on the web. Blockbuster dis­missed it as a niche until Netflix had 4.2 mil­lion sub­scribers by 2004. {#subscribers}
## Streaming too soon
In 2007, when in­ter­net speeds and screens made stream­ing seem un­fea­si­ble, Netflix moved into it any­way. {086-S10}
Five or six years later came orig­i­nal shows such as *House of Cards*, with whole sea­sons dropped at once. Binge-watching be­came the norm.
Kodak, by con­trast, saw dig­i­tal pho­tog­ra­phy com­ing and pro­tected its mar­ket. BlackBerry was sure peo­ple wanted key­boards, and Nokia was dis­rupted too. {086-C07}
~ The con­ven­tional think­ing about short at­ten­tion spans is wrong, Varma said, point­ing to the many com­ments on a ten-and-a-half-hour episode he recorded with Ajay Shah. {#tenhalf}

quote.text: But in­ter­nally a big com­pany is al­ways doing the safe thing and pro­tect­ing its mar­ket. And why would I dis­rupt my­self?

sections.label: The four pillars
sections.head: Weirdos welcome
sections.caption: where disruptors come from
body: Where do dis­rup­tors come from? Ajay Shah of­fered four pil­lars.

The first is cul­ture. Societies that reg­i­ment chil­dren and hound them into com­pet­i­tive exams pro­duce con­form­ists. Without a cul­ture of ir­rev­er­ence, he said, “you’re just going to be­come a banker”. A more easy­go­ing cul­ture tol­er­ates heretics. “Very many peo­ple will go off to the beaches of Goa and get doped out, but a small frac­tion of them will be­come amaz­ing peo­ple.” {086-J12}

The sec­ond is the gate­keep­ers: al­lo­ca­tors of ven­ture cap­i­tal, re­search fund­ing, jour­nal space, patents and li­cences. If ed­i­tors re­ward con­formism, re­searchers end up “pol­ish­ing the apple”. {086-C11}
## Failure, and the weirdos
The third is to em­brace sur­vivor­ship bias. “You have to throw a hun­dred darts at so­ci­ety and two of them will work out,” Shah said. That does not make the two ge­niuses. {086-C12}

The fourth is that truly dis­rup­tive peo­ple are often not nice. {086-C13} Alexander Solzhenitsyn, up close, was not a good human being, Shah said, and had there been so­cial media in Newton’s time, his writ­ing would have looked cringe­wor­thy.

~ Amit Varma added that Silicon Valley works partly be­cause its cul­ture makes it okay to fail. He praised Emergent Ventures for fund­ing those whom con­ven­tional al­lo­ca­tors miss: “the freaks” and “the nut­cases”. {086-J14}

quote.text: So more sti­fling so­ci­eties just make stul­ti­fied peo­ple and we are less likely to get think­ing from them.

sections.label: The machines
sections.head: Error, or eureka?
sections.caption: what language models cannot yet find
body: In the show’s sec­ond episode Ajay Shah had asked whether AI could come up with some­thing as dras­tic as the the­ory of rel­a­tiv­ity. Amit Varma re­turned to the ques­tion.
The pod­caster Dwarkesh Patel had asked why lan­guage mod­els, with the en­tire cor­pus of human knowl­edge mem­o­rised, have not made a sin­gle new con­nec­tion that led to a dis­cov­ery. {086-R29}

A user called Michael replied: “To an LLM, a novel dis­cov­ery is in­dis­tin­guish­able from an error.” Varma saw a grain of truth in it, but AI is not only LLMs, he said, and will one day make dis­cov­er­ies. {086-C15}
## Ajay Shah’s law

Shah of­fered a law: if an LLM can write it, it is not worth writ­ing. {086-C16} He tried to get one to pro­duce, from a one-paragraph prompt, a paper on why India’s FRBM failed. It could not, so the paper was worth writ­ing.
Varma, a power user, pushed back. By Sturgeon’s law, he said, 95 per cent of ev­ery­thing is crap, so de­fault out­put will be too. {086-J20} Used well, the tools are “mind blow­ing” for re­search.
~ Shah does use the paid Google Gemini. Asked to find flaws in a news­pa­per col­umn, it gave five sug­ges­tions “like what a mas­ter ed­i­tor would do”. {086-R32}

quote.text: If you can sup­ply a prompt and the LLM can write the paper, then you should just pub­lish it as the prompt.
Thinking out­side the box is a nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient con­di­tion. You also need luck, but you also need per­sis­tence be­cause that is how you in­crease your sur­face area of serendip­ity.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Four tales of rule-breakers, bad timing and a DVD that never arrived

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the doctor who catheterised himself in 1929
stories.head: A man after his own heart
body: In Berlin in 1929, catheters had just come into use and early an­giog­ra­phy of other or­gans had begun. {#berlin1929} But the con­ven­tional wis­dom, Amit Varma said, was that you went nowhere near the heart.

Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doc­tor, be­lieved a catheter could be taken into the heart. His su­pe­rior for­bade the ex­per­i­ment. Forssmann agreed with part of the cau­tion: he would not put some­thing in some­one else’s heart. He would put it in his own. {086-S04}
His nurse, who was de­voted to him, would not hear of it. He was too im­por­tant, she said, and he should ex­per­i­ment on her in­stead.

He strapped her down and gave her a local anaes­thetic. Then, while she waited, he slid the catheter into his own arm and guided it up the vein with a mir­ror. By the time she re­alised she had been duped, it was a done deal.
They walked to the X-ray lab, where, with a flu­o­ro­scope, he guided the catheter into the right atrium of his heart. He did it nine more times on him­self, and lost his job. {#ninemore}

At the next hos­pi­tal Ferdinand Sauerbruch sneered that such ex­per­i­ments be­longed in a cir­cus. By 1932, Varma said, Forssmann’s game was over and he had moved to urol­ogy. He joined the Nazi party and spent five years im­pris­oned after the war, a part of the story Varma called ir­rel­e­vant, be­cause he al­ways sep­a­rates art and artist.
~ Meanwhile, oth­ers went deeper into his work. In the 1950s Forssmann won a Nobel Prize. {#nobel} He died in 1979, at 75, of a heart at­tack.
stories.why: A pro­ce­dure Amit Varma went through fully con­scious in 2025 began with one young Berlin doc­tor bet­ting his own body against the con­sen­sus, and pay­ing for it with his ca­reer. Varma, who calls him Werner, feels close to him.
stories.postscript: Narendra Shenoy told Varma this story while he was in hos­pi­tal. {#shenoy}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Werner Forssmann’s self-experiment

stories.kicker: A salesman’s memory of Charles Dotter, as read by Amit Varma
stories.head: Lend me your blowtorch
body: At a con­fer­ence in the early 1960s, Bill Cook, a trav­el­ling sales­man, no­ticed a short, mus­cu­lar, bald man with dart­ing eyes sit­ting on a box be­hind his stall. He made Cook ner­vous.

Just be­fore clos­ing, the stranger asked to bor­row Cook’s blow­torch and some Teflon tub­ing, to prac­tise mak­ing catheters in his hotel room. Cook thought he had “a real space cadet” on his hands, but agreed, and asked his name. It was Charles Dotter, who often as­sem­bled catheters in his own kitchen. {#kitchen}

“The next morn­ing he was wait­ing for me with ten beau­ti­fully made Teflon catheters and my blow­torch,” Cook re­called. {086-S06} They were sold that day for ten dol­lars each, and Cook called Dotter “my first pro­duc­tion em­ployee”.
~ Cook, who had just started his busi­ness, went on to found the leader in an­gio­plasty equip­ment.
stories.why: Dotter was not just a thinker rea­son­ing from first prin­ci­ples and try­ing to con­vince peo­ple, Amit Varma said. He was a doer, mak­ing the things him­self and car­ry­ing out the ex­per­i­ments.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Charles Dotter and the borrowed blowtorch

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s music start-up, pitched in New York in 2000
stories.head: Right idea, wrong year
body: In 1999, in his early twen­ties, Amit Varma was shown the godown of Magnasound, Shashi Gopal’s label be­hind Daler Mehndi, Alisha Chinai and Baba Sehgal. It held thou­sands of CDs, and Gopal told him to take what he wanted. {#godown}

Varma told him that in ten years they would be worth­less, be­cause all music would be dig­i­tal and sold on­line. He con­vinced Gopal and Sunil Mengrajani, Gopal’s head of mar­ket­ing, and the three be­came equal part­ners in Sonictown.
In the Napster era la­bels wanted to crush dig­i­tal music. Even so, Mengrajani se­cured rights to 80,000 songs from American la­bels. {#tracks}

In early 2000, be­fore a room of New York in­vestors, Varma pitched on­line song sales and pages where mu­si­cians could con­nect and up­date fans. {086-S12} The room was ex­cited. Then the Nasdaq crashed.
~ Business World gave it a dou­ble spread.

quote.text: I laid out what was ba­si­cally MySpace and I laid out what was ba­si­cally iTunes.

stories.postscript: A sec­ond ven­ture later left Varma deeply in debt, which, he said, is a story for an­other time.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Sonictown, his start-up that came too early

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Govind Nihalani and a film lost to inertia
stories.head: The director’s missing Party
body: Around 2010 the di­rec­tor Govind Nihalani wanted to film Amit Varma’s 2009 novel, a book Varma calls bad. Varma naively tried to talk him out of it, then helped write a treat­ment.

Nobody would fund it, though Nihalani had made *Ardh Satya* and *Tamas*. At his sug­ges­tion Varma set a ver­sion in Pune, for the Marathi in­dus­try. Then he lost touch, too em­bar­rassed to re­con­nect.

Nihalani had once told him his one re­gret: he had no copy of his own film *Party*. {086-S11} Varma’s friend Ved Sharma in New York found it on Netflix, kept the disc, paid the charge and posted it. By then in­er­tia had set in, and it never reached Nihalani.
~ Varma be­lieves Nihalani got a copy else­where. Ajay Shah wor­ried that in the mean­time DVD play­ers had van­ished from the world. {#dvdplayers}
stories.why: Even a di­rec­tor of Nihalani’s stature could not get an in­de­pen­dent film funded, Varma said. And Netflix’s cat­a­logue held a film its maker could not find in his own coun­try.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Govind Nihalani’s missing film

quiz.q: What test told Amit Varma that he had already had a minor heart attack?
quiz.a: An HS tro­ponin test, for a pro­tein the heart re­leases dur­ing an at­tack.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma spend a day or two in ICU before his stent?
quiz.a: He was al­ler­gic to as­pirin, which he must take daily for life with a stent.

quiz.q: What did Barry Marshall drink to prove that stomach ulcers are an infectious disease?
quiz.a: Water con­tain­ing Helicobacter py­lori; then he cured the ul­cers with a course of an­tibi­otics.

quiz.q: Which two lower-order batsmen did Sri Lanka send out to open at the 1996 World Cup?
quiz.a: Romesh Kaluwitharana and Sanath Jayasuriya, told to go hard from the very first ball.

quiz.q: In what year did Netflix move into streaming, and why did that seem absurd?
quiz.a: In 2007, when in­ter­net speeds and screens were too poor for watch­ing films.

quiz.q: What law did Ajay Shah propose for testing whether a paper is worth writing?
quiz.a: If an LLM can write it from a prompt, it is not worth writ­ing.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 86. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Werner Forssmann (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain); Barry Marshall (WikiEdtingProfile2021, CC BY-SA 4.0); Ferdinand Sauerbruch (Heinscher, CC BY-SA 3.0 de); Sanath Jayasuriya (User:Chamal_N, CC BY 2.0); Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (Bert Verhoeff for Anefo, CC0); Tyler Cowen (Tyler Cowen, CC BY-SA 3.0); Govind Nihalani (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5).

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: Morgan Brown’s tweet on DeepSeek
shelf.creator: Morgan Brown
shelf.why: Its line, ‘Incumbents op­ti­mize ex­ist­ing pro­cesses while dis­rup­tors re­think the fun­da­men­tal approach’, is the episode’s the­sis in one sen­tence.

shelf.title: Objects From Our Past (Episode 77)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It was his idea, and he says it’s an episode he ‘absolutely’ loves.

shelf.title: Is the Singularity Near? (Episode 2)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ early episode on AI, with Amit’s ar­gu­ment that AGI is about five years away and eas­ier to reach than peo­ple as­sume.

shelf.title: Sagar Shah’s interview with Ashwin Subramanian
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: It backs the claim that an Indian tin­kerer did it first.

shelf.title: Ashwin interviewed by ChessBase
shelf.creator: ChessBase
shelf.why: More on the un­sung in­no­va­tor be­hind a now-famous broad­cast fea­ture.

shelf.title: Peter Leko and Judit Polgar on Gukesh’s heart rate
shelf.creator: Peter Leko and Judit Polgar
shelf.why: A vivid ex­am­ple of com­po­sure under pres­sure made vis­i­ble.

shelf.title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Episode 19)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s con­trar­ian ideas on cricket strat­egy and tac­tics, first de­vel­oped in 2008 and still not well un­der­stood, which he says hold truly novel in­sights.

shelf.title: Opportunity, Choice and the IPL (2008)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit is proud of it for pre­dict­ing, be­fore the fact, that the IPL would rev­o­lu­tionise cricket, res­cue Test cricket, and cre­ate com­pe­ti­tion for tal­ent de­spite the BCCI being a monop­sony.

shelf.title: The lesson from this IPL: Front-load your innings (2014)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s orig­i­nal ar­gu­ment that T20 teams should drop the pinch-consolidate-slog gram­mar in­her­ited from ODIs: send the hit­ters in first, keep at­tack­ing for all twenty overs and hold the an­chor back for emer­gen­cies.

shelf.title: National Highway 420 (and the EV of Aggressive Batting) (2016)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn ap­ply­ing ex­pected value to cricket: ag­gres­sive bat­ting pays, and teams bat­ting first were sys­tem­at­i­cally un­der­es­ti­mat­ing the par score.

shelf.title: My Friend Sancho
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s own novel, which he dis­misses as slight (‘a bad novel I don’t talk about much’) while grant­ing that its premise was strong; it comes up in his story about Nihalani and Marathi cin­ema.

shelf.title: Ardh Satya
shelf.creator: Govind Nihalani
shelf.why: It shows the director’s stature, which makes it strik­ing that he couldn’t get an in­de­pen­dent film funded.

shelf.title: Party
shelf.creator: Govind Nihalani
shelf.why: Amit holds it up as a land­mark of Nihalani’s ca­reer.

shelf.title: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s fullest think­ing on the craft of pod­cast­ing, which Ajay says also ex­plains how the mod­ern media and cre­ative economies work.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: Underrated, Overrated, Complicated (Episode 85)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ un­der­rated-overrated-complicated episode, in­clud­ing round one of their de­bate on Twitter (Ajay: a cesspool; Amit: a gift if you cu­rate your feed) and the setup for Amit’s story of early fail­ure with Sonictown.

shelf.title: The 2000 Business World article on Sonictown
shelf.creator: Business World
shelf.why: The sur­viv­ing trace of a ven­ture that oth­er­wise left no mark on the in­ter­net.

shelf.title: The Surface Area of Serendipity (Episode 39)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It’s the fuller case for per­sis­tence and bias for ac­tion as the way to give luck more chances to find you.

shelf.title: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts go under the hood on how Newton and Gandhi emerged, trac­ing their in­tel­lec­tual in­flu­ences rather than judg­ing them by their high­light reels.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why re­search fund­ing in India is ‘a truly bad space’, and the al­ter­na­tive: an in­dus­try-neutral ap­proach that con­tracts R&D out through grants to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms rather than hav­ing bu­reau­crats pick sec­tors.

shelf.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Episode 8)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the bright­est peo­ple con­cen­trate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a clus­ter be­comes a mag­net for more tal­ent, helped by friendly reg­u­la­tion and a cul­ture where it is okay to fail.

shelf.title: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s deep dive into the bot­tom-up story of Unix and free soft­ware, built by peo­ple work­ing for decades with no promised re­ward.

shelf.title: Shruti Rajagopalan Remembers the Angle of the Light (Episode 410 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It’s ‘pre­cisely on this subject’: she’s a dis­rup­tor in how cap­i­tal is al­lo­cated.

shelf.title: Emergent Ventures India
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: No monthly or yearly tar­gets, no blame for fail­ure.

shelf.title: Emergent Ventures
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: Tyler Cowen’s grant pro­gramme, the orig­i­nal model for fund­ing un­con­ven­tional in­di­vid­u­als; Amit finds it won­der­ful that it backs mad ideas from peo­ple with no cre­den­tials.

shelf.title: Dwarkesh Patel’s tweet on why LLMs haven’t made discoveries
shelf.creator: Dwarkesh Patel
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great ques­tion, one Dwarkesh said no­body had an­swered sat­is­fac­to­rily, and it sharp­ens the human-vs-AI nov­elty de­bate.

shelf.title: Michael’s response to Dwarkesh Patel
shelf.creator: Michael
shelf.why: It ar­gues that to an LLM a novel dis­cov­ery is in­dis­tin­guish­able from an error.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah’s paper on why the Indian FRBM failed
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The LLMs couldn’t, which by his own law proved it was worth writ­ing.

shelf.title: Google Gemini (paid)
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: It gave five good sug­ges­tions ‘like what a mas­ter ed­i­tor would do’, and he signed up for $20 a month that day.

shelf.title: Perplexity (Pro)
shelf.creator: Perplexity
shelf.why: A ‘mind blowing’ learn­ing tool: it an­swers bet­ter than search or Wikipedia and nudges you to­wards the right ques­tions and down re­ward­ing rab­bit holes.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Amit on his hos­pi­tal bill: ‘this can be a per­pet­ual heart at­tack machine’. You have a heart at­tack, get the pro­ce­dure, see the bill, have an­other heart at­tack, and so on, with the game-theoretic catch that the sur­geon must keep you alive long enough to pay the next bill. Ajay di­ag­noses ‘Zeno-phobia’, ‘the ir­ra­tional fear of con­ver­gent sequences’, after Zeno’s para­dox. Amit: ‘This is the finest anal­y­sis of a bad joke I have ever seen. Sashtang pranam.’

Sudhir Sarnobat called Ajay to say the pro­ce­dure went well and re­ported back that Ajay is ‘an ex­tremely ex­pres­sion­less man. I said I’m Sudhir speak­ing and he just said okay.’ Amit had imag­ined Ajay see­ing Sudhir’s name flash on the caller ID and con­clud­ing Amit was dead.
Lancelot Pinto’s ver­dict on Amit’s lungs: ‘These might even be the best lungs in South Asia, Ajay Shah. Not his words, mine.’

Ferdinand Sauerbruch’s dis­missal of Forssmann, Amit’s em­blem of the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional minded: ‘With such ex­per­i­ments you might ha­bil­i­tate in a cir­cus, but these have no place in a de­cent German hos­pi­tal.’

Amit de­scribes his own an­gio­plasty as a video game: three screens be­side him like a day trader’s setup, a doc­tor with what is prac­ti­cally a game con­troller, and, ‘like in a game of Pac-Man’, ma­noeu­vring through the ar­ter­ies zap­ping clots.
